name: River Plate 1941–47 (La Máquina)
scopeNote: River Plate's 'La Máquina' from its first match as the named forward line, 21 Sep 1941 (4-0 at Independiente, three goals by Pedernera; La Página Millonaria and Los Andes), to the end of the core group in 1947 (Los Andes: the base was kept 'hasta 1947 inclusive'; Pedernera left for Atlanta in 1946). Pedernera had been moved to centre-forward mid-season in 1941 (El Gráfico, via search summary only). Style named in the evidence: a 'rough W-M' with withdrawn inside-forwards (Wilson, retrospective), short passing and possession (La Página Millonaria, 1941 match report via a 2011 article; Muñoz, undated). 'Total football' and 'precursor of Clockwork Orange' appear only as later retrospective labels (Wikipedia, Los Andes, Game of the People) and are not the period's own terms.
openQuestions: Managers: the official coach list (en.wikipedia List of Club Atlético River Plate managers) gives Cesarini 1940-07-07 to 1944-10-22 and Peucelle 1944-10-29 to 1946-12-08. Peucelle's role in 1941-44 was de facto (Game of the People: he became a de facto coach after Plattkó's M-defence failed; FIFA and Wikipedia-mirror summaries say he proposed moving Pedernera). The managers[] entries use the official dates; confirm whether to record Peucelle's de facto period from 1941 instead. Cesarini's en.wikipedia body text says 1941-44, the table says 1940-44; the table was used.

Shape conflict: Wilson (SI, 2015, retrospective) describes a 'rough W-M' with Néstor Rossi as attacking centre-half; La Página Millonaria (2011) quotes the 1941 line-up as 'dos defensores, tres mediocampistas y ¡cinco delanteros!' (2-3-5). Both are recorded; the period-specific 2-3-5 quote is undated in the article text.

Marking (mar): the only marking fact is Yácono's personal man-marking ('The Stamp', Wilson). No source says whether River's press or block was zonal or man-oriented. The mar axis therefore rests on a single individual-level fact through defensive-block.

Pressing, transitions and set pieces have no verified fact. El Gráfico's 1941-45 history (Juvenal, ch. IX) and the Peucelle retrospective (El Gráfico 'Humilde y millonario') returned 403, so the most likely sources for these are not yet read.

Nickname origin conflicts: Wikipedia and Los Andes credit Borocotó (El Gráfico, 1942, after the 6-2 win over Chacarita, 12 June 1942). Peucelle is quoted (Los Andes, undated) saying it was 'un invento de Doña Rosa, la mamá de Adolfo Pedernera', and FIFA says Peucelle later revealed that the nickname came from Pedernera's mother Rosa. Both are kept; check the El Gráfico 1942 piece before choosing.

Credit for the switch of Pedernera to centre-forward: FIFA (Tighe, 2020) says 'Opinion is still divided as to whether Peucelle or Cesarini should get the credit'. Peucelle's suggestion appears only in search summaries (La Capital, Mar del Plata; a Wikipedia mirror) and is not verified on a page.

Period end: 'until 1947 inclusive' (Los Andes) and 'around 1941 to 1947' (Wilson) versus Pedernera's exit in 1946 and Peucelle's exit on 1946-12-08. The profile uses the partial year 1947; the day is not fixed.
Debuts of Di Stéfano and Carrizo in the team are named on Los Andes without a year. The year 1945 is expected but was not read on a page, so the squad-building fact is recorded as verified: false.

No primary quote from Cesarini or Peucelle on their own football was found. The only Peucelle quote is attributed (Los Andes, 2020) and the Cesarini 'authority' phrase is from Wikipedia, not a period quote.

sources.title: Pedernera, the 'twinkle-toed engine driver' (Sam Tighe)
sources.evidence: Page read via the page reader (the www.fifa.com URL returned empty). Coaches Cesarini and Peucelle 'switch[ed] him to a more central and withdrawn role and invit[ed] him to alternate between driving into the box to finish moves off and sitting back to direct them' (1941). The team had 'five forwards capable of swapping positions and popping up in places where the opposition least expected them'. 'Opinion is still divided as to whether Peucelle or Cesarini should get the credit.' Article date 2020-05-12 taken from the Wikipedia citation for this article, not the page.

sources.title: Pedernera, the 'twinkle-toed engine driver' (Sam Tighe)
sources.evidence: Pedernera 'dreamed up passes that no-one else saw' and 'had a vision of the pitch that no-one else possessed'. Debut at 16 in 1935; left River in 1946. Describes the player, not the period; the adjectives are the writer's.

sources.title: La Máquina
sources.evidence: Undated wiki page; accessedOn used as articleDate. Core forwards: Juan Carlos Muñoz, José Manuel Moreno, Adolfo Pedernera, Ángel Labruna and Félix Loustau. 'For their dynamism and rotating positions', the team is 'often considered a precursor of the famous' Dutch 'Clockwork Orange' side of the 1970s. Retrospective label only; the page cites Wilson, Goal and Galeano for it.

sources.title: Renato Cesarini
sources.evidence: Undated wiki page; accessedOn used as articleDate. 'With River, Cesarini became known for his authority on all matters pertaining to the sport'; known as 'La Biblia del fútbol'. The page gives no tactics for him. Spell dates: body says 'coach from 1941 to 1944', infobox says 1939-1944, the manager list says 1940-44 (see openQuestions).

sources.title: A 70 años del primer partido de La Máquina
sources.evidence: Debut day, 21 Sep 1941: 'El objetivo de aquel equipo era tener la posesión de la pelota', preceded by 'una brillante muestra de fútbol de pases cortos'. Match: River 4-0 at Independiente, three goals by Pedernera and one by Muñoz. Fan-site article, quoting the period's match reporting without naming the original.

sources.title: A 70 años del primer partido de La Máquina
sources.evidence: Build-up aim: 'toque preciso y comenzar bien la jugada desde la defensa'.

sources.title: A 70 años del primer partido de La Máquina
sources.evidence: Line-up shape: 'formaba con dos defensores, tres mediocampistas y ¡cinco delanteros!' (2-3-5). Conflicts with Wilson's 'rough W-M' (see openQuestions).

sources.title: Los Andes: 'Un día como hoy nació La Máquina de River'
sources.evidence: Birth date 'el 21 de septiembre de 1941', with Cesarini as coach; Pedernera played as centre-forward after that match. Pedernera 'bajaba' from a nominal 9 to midfield to organise play with Moreno, who moved to 8 after Labruna took the 10 role. Retrospective description; no date for the positional change.

sources.title: Los Andes: 'Un día como hoy nació La Máquina de River' (Labruna)
sources.evidence: Labruna 'se destacaba por su velocidad y por aprovechar los espacios para recibir pases en cortada y definir'. Retrospective description.

sources.title: Los Andes: 'Un día como hoy nació La Máquina de River' (debuts)
sources.evidence: The page names Alfredo Di Stéfano and Amadeo Carrizo as debutants 'en ese equipo' but gives no year. The year 1945 is expected from general knowledge and was not read on a page, so verified is false.

sources.title: Los Andes: Peucelle on the name 'La Máquina'
sources.evidence: Peucelle, 'en una ocasión': 'La Máquina de River fue un invento de Doña Rosa, la mamá de Adolfo Pedernera'. Undated in the article. Recorded as an attributed quote in statedView; this source entry is not verified for stated-view.

sources.title: Game of the People: River Plate 1940s – it takes a team to tango
sources.evidence: 'Peucelle also had a habit of moving players around to exploit their strengths' (undated). Peucelle became a de facto coach 'after the failure of Ferenc Plattkó to introduce the so-called M-defence' (no date given). Retrospective, one author.

sources.title: Game of the People: River Plate 1940s – it takes a team to tango
sources.evidence: 'they seemed to be in no hurry to score but preferred instead to outpass their opponents' (no date given; describes the early 1940s side).

sources.title: What if they met? River Plate's La Máquina, Il Grande Torino (Jonathan Wilson)
sources.evidence: 'They played a rough W-M shape with an attacking center half in Néstor Rossi'; 'Rather than the two inside-forwards withdrawing as was usual in a W-M, it was Moreno and Pedernera who dropped off into the space in front of the half line.' Wilson dates the side to 'around 1941 to 1947'. Retrospective analysis by the author of Inverting the Pyramid.

sources.title: What if they met? River Plate's La Máquina, Il Grande Torino (Jonathan Wilson)
sources.evidence: Loustau 'patrolled the whole of the left flank', and 'Loustau's running meant that the left-half could shuffle across.' Retrospective.

sources.title: What if they met? River Plate's La Máquina, Il Grande Torino (Jonathan Wilson)
sources.evidence: Centre-half 'first Rodolfi and then Rossi' moved right, 'allowing Norberto Yácono, the nominal right-half, a more defensive brief'. Yácono became known as 'The Stamp' 'for the way he would stick to the player he was marking'. This is an individual man-marking fact, not a team-level zonal or man statement.

sources.title: What if they met? River Plate's La Máquina, Il Grande Torino (Jonathan Wilson)
sources.evidence: Muñoz (undated): 'We went out on the pitch and played our way: take the ball, give it to me'; 'There was no rush. It was instinctive.' Rival Lazzatti: 'You play against La Máquina with the intention of winning.' Quotes are undated in the article.

statedView.quote: La Máquina de River fue un invento de Doña Rosa, la mamá de Adolfo Pedernera

influences.note: On-pitch exemplar of La Nuestra / Rioplatense; Wilson: it defined 'what came to be perceived as the true Argentinian style, la nuestra' (SI, 2015).

confidence.reason: Mostly retrospective evidence on one team: the period-specific facts are the 1941 match report summarised by a 2011 fan site, a 2020 FIFA article and undated quotes; the W-M (Wilson) and 2-3-5 (La Página Millonaria) shapes conflict; the Juvenal and Peucelle El Gráfico pieces returned 403. No pressing, transition or set-piece fact, and no marking fact at team level.
